extracted.intended_audience: educated public and policymakers (late-18th-century British readership)
extracted.subtask_description: A conservative political essay arguing that manners, religion, and established institutions are essential for social cohesion and warning against the destructive effects of revolutionary 'light' and abstract reason. It evaluates the moral and practical consequences of overthrowing traditional structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of chivalry and refined manners
rubrics_metrics.description: This mixed system of opinion and sentiment (originating in ancient chivalry) gave modern Europe its character and produced a noble equality that softened pride and power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve the 'spirit of a gentleman' and the social manners that 'mitigated kings into companions, and raised private men to be fellows with kings.' Its extinction will be a great loss; manners create a soft collar on sovereigns and supply civilizing, ennobling effects that reduce grossness in vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws should be supported by affections and manners, not terror alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions require public affections and manners as supplements and correctives; laws supported only by terror and private interest are inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid a legal regime that relies solely on penalties and instrumental calculations. Cultivate love, veneration, admiration, and attachment so institutions are embodied in persons and thus capable of commanding voluntary respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason that banishes affections is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: A kind of reason which banishes the affections is incapable of filling their place in society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not adopt a 'mechanic philosophy' that excludes the moral sentiments; policies and constitutions should account for human affections and the need for moral imagination. Anti-pattern: treating people as pure calculators of private interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prejudices/tradition have practical moral value
rubrics_metrics.description: Prejudice (long-standing prejudices and customs) often contains latent wisdom and gives steadiness to virtue: 'Prejudice renders a man's virtue his habit, and not a series of unconnected acts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about discarding traditional prejudices wholesale; they provide ready application in emergencies, engage the mind in a steady course of action, and turn duty into habit. Reformers should seek the wisdom within customs rather than abolish them by abstract reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion is the basis of civil society
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion is the foundation for civilization and moral life; 'we know, and, what is better, we feel inwardly, that religion is the basis of civil society.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain established religious institutions as sources of comfort and moral guidance. Reject replacing religion with atheism or 'uncouth superstition' born from the void left by removing religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve established institutions (church, monarchy, aristocracy) in their degree
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than abolishing establishments, keep an established church, an established monarchy, an established aristocracy, and an established democracy, each to the degree it exists and in no greater.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reform should not mean wholesale destruction of social pillars. Policy must respect historical continuity and the existing balance among institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public admiration and manners make a country lovable
rubrics_metrics.description: To make us love our country, our country ought to be lovely; a system of manners in every nation makes the nation relishable to a well-formed mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate public affections and cultural refinements so civic loyalty is rooted in sentiment as well as utility. Anti-pattern: making institutions purely instrumental and unlovable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerate slow, prudent change rather than fashionable innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who destroy old schemes because they are old are misguided; duration and attachment have value and sudden, hasty building up of new schemes is suspect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach institutional change with prudence; distrust reformers who equate novelty with improvement. Rapid experiments risk losing foundational supports (commerce, learning, manners).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commerce, arts, and learning depend on traditional protectors
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning, commerce, trade, and manufacture grew under the shade of nobility and religion and may decay if their natural protecting principles are removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protect the social and institutional context (patronage, clergy, nobility) that historically sustained arts and industry. Beware of reforms that undermine those protectors and thereby imperil cultural and economic flourishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of political calculation that justifies crime for advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: Justifying regicide, parricide, or sacrilege as mere homicide or permissible if beneficial leads to a system where criminal means are preferred because they are shorter and expedient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject utilitarian calculations that weigh crimes against contingent benefits; tolerating such justification erodes natural sense of wrong and right and will promote perfidy, murder, and corruption of public morality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre as a school for moral sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Theatre, dealing with audiences' natural impulses, is a better school of moral sentiments than churches where feelings of humanity are outraged by revolutionary exultation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use art and drama to cultivate moral intuitions that reject Machiavellian maxims. Anti-pattern: intellectual exultation at crimes as means to political ends that would be rejected by a theatric moral sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice should be grave, decorous, and dignified
rubrics_metrics.description: The punishment of real tyrants is noble and consolatory when done with dignity; justice 'in its punishments rather seems to submit to a necessity than to make a choice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mob, theatrical, or vindictive spectacles of punishment. Even when punishing atrocity, preserve solemnity and decorum—don't degrade justice into revenge or performative triumph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconsistency in degrading then entrusting individuals undermines prudence
rubrics_metrics.description: To degrade and insult a man as the worst of criminals and afterwards trust him in highest concerns is inconsistent in reasoning and imprudent in policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure coherence between accusations and subsequent choices: if someone is publicly proclaimed infamous, do not then place public trust in them. Practically, avoid political contradictions that reduce credibility and safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventive cruelty and confiscation follow destruction of traditional bonds
rubrics_metrics.description: When fealty and chivalrous spirit are extinct, power will resort to preventive murder and preventive confiscation—grim maxims of power not standing on its own honor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain social bonds of honor and fealty as safeguards against a slide to arbitrary preventive violence and predatory state practices. Anti-pattern: building power on fear and appetite rather than on honor and esteem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual cabals detached from tradition are dangerous when organized
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual freethinkers were harmless; but a philosophic cabal acting collectively to influence public affairs is a novel and dangerous phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary when small intellectual factions attempt to become political forces; their collective action can destabilize institutions in ways isolated writers never could. Preserve plural, independent sources of authority rather than concentrated avant-garde factions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural human feelings (pity, terror) are instructive to reason
rubrics_metrics.description: We are made to be affected by melancholy sentiments at spectacles of fortune's uncertainty; 'our passions instruct our reason' and such feelings purify the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow moral emotions to inform political judgment. Anti-pattern: suppressing natural pity and terror as irrelevant to political decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid substituting abstract rights for embodied social relations
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'rights of man' abstracted into doctrine dissolve the decent drapery of life and treat kings and women as mere animals; abstract reason can destroy the moral imagination that dignifies society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground political rights and reform in lived social relations and historical context rather than abstract universal formulas that may strip institutions of their moral coverings and generate social barbarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: National character and long habit matter for political stability
rubrics_metrics.description: England's 'sullen resistance to innovation' and national character preserve generosity, dignity, religion, and civility; sudden imitation of foreign revolutionary models is dangerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect national particularities and inherited habits when considering reforms. Anti-pattern: copying foreign political experiments without regard to local manners and institutions.
